title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Laboratory Knowledge & Skills - Biotechnology - Agarose gel electrophoresis
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: Agarose gel electrophoresis is a fundamental technique used to isolate genetic material. It separates DNA molecules by forcing them through a porous matrix primarily based on which two fundamental physical characteristics of the DNA?
options: Molecular weight (size) and inherent negative electrical charge
G-C base pair ratio and complex secondary folding structures
Intrinsic radioactivity and hydrophobic molecular interactions
Isoelectric point and localized positive electrical charges
questions.explain:
Agarose gel electrophoresis separates molecules based on **charge and size (molecular weight)**. 

The phosphate groups embedded in the DNA backbone give the molecule a uniform **negative electrical charge**. When an electric current is applied, the DNA is universally drawn toward the positive electrode (anode). Because the agarose forms a dense web-like matrix, smaller fragments can navigate the pores easily and travel faster, while larger fragments get tangled and lag behind, separating the DNA strictly by its size.
questions.subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: A researcher needs to resolve two very small, closely sized PCR products ($150 \text{ bp}$ and $175 \text{ bp}$) on a gel. To achieve the highest visual resolution and effectively separate these two bands, how should the researcher adjust the standard gel pouring protocol?
options: Decrease the applied running voltage to less than $10 \text{ V}$.
Use a significantly lower concentration of agarose (e.g., $0.5\%$) so the fragments can travel completely unimpeded.
Use a significantly higher concentration of agarose (e.g., $2.0\%$) to create a tighter matrix with smaller pores.
Omit the DNA loading dye entirely, as the heavy glycerol will artificially weigh down small fragments.
questions.explain:
The concentration of agarose directly dictates the pore size of the resulting gel matrix. 

Lower concentrations (e.g., $0.7\%-1.0\%$) have large pores and are ideal for large genomic fragments. Higher concentrations (e.g., $2.0\%-3.0\%$) create a much tighter, denser matrix (Option 'c'). This dense matrix increases the friction acting against the DNA fragments, which is essential to create enough "drag" to successfully tease apart very small, similarly sized fragments like a $150 \text{ bp}$ and $175 \text{ bp}$ band.

questions.q: Prior to pipetting DNA samples into the wells of an agarose gel, a technician mixes each sample with a small volume of a $6\times$ Loading Dye. What is the primary dual purpose of using this standard loading dye?
options: To permanently stain the DNA backbone for UV visualization and to buffer the pH of the sample.
To provide density (via glycerol) so the sample sinks into the well, and to provide visible color tracking fronts to monitor the run.
To covalently attach fluorescent tags to the DNA and digest any contaminating RNA molecules.
To carry the electrical current into the well and prevent the localized heating of the agarose matrix.
questions.explain:
Loading dyes serve two mechanical purposes: 
1. **Density:** They contain heavy sugar derivatives like glycerol or Ficoll, which weigh the DNA sample down so it drops neatly into the submerged well rather than floating away into the running buffer. 
2. **Visual Tracking:** They contain colored dyes (like bromophenol blue or xylene cyanol) that run ahead of or alongside the DNA, allowing the technician to monitor the progress of the electrophoresis run with the naked eye. 
> The dye does *not* stain the DNA itself for final visualization; that is the job of intercalating dyes like Ethidium Bromide.
questions.subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: To visualize the separated DNA fragments after running a gel, the agarose must contain an intercalating agent like Ethidium Bromide (EtBr), SYBR Safe, or GelRed. How does a chemical intercalating dye interact with the DNA molecule to permit visualization?
options: It covalently bonds to the exposed terminal 5' phosphate group of each strand, creating a luminescent tail.
It slides physically between the stacked nitrogenous base pairs of the DNA double helix.
It rapidly degrades the sugar-phosphate backbone, releasing measurable bursts of fluorescent photons in the process.
It binds strictly to the short, single-stranded primer overhangs created during the PCR cycles.
questions.explain:
The term **intercalation** refers to the physical insertion of a molecule into the spaces between other structures. 

Dyes like Ethidium Bromide feature planar (flat) chemical ring structures that perfectly match the spacing between the "rungs" of the DNA ladder. They slide directly between the stacked, complementary nitrogenous bases of double-stranded DNA. Once trapped inside the hydrophobic interior of the helix, the dye's fluorescence is massively amplified when exposed to UV light, allowing scientists to see the bands.

questions.q: A student connects an electrophoresis chamber to a standard DC power supply and runs a gel for 45 minutes. Upon placing the gel on a UV transilluminator, the student discovers that all the sample wells are entirely empty and no DNA bands are visible on the gel. Upon reviewing their setup, what mechanical error most likely caused the DNA to run backward out of the wells and into the buffer?
options: The gel was accidentally cast using distilled water rather than standard TAE buffer.
The agarose concentration was drastically too high, causing a physical blockade.
The power supply electrodes were reversed, placing the positive red anode directly behind the wells.
The student set the power supply to AC (alternating current) instead of DC (direct current).
questions.explain:
DNA is negatively charged and will unequivocally travel toward the positive pole (the red anode). 

The standard phrase in biotechnology is **"Run toward red."** The wells must be positioned near the negative pole (the black cathode). If a student plugs the lid in backward, positioning the positive red electrode *behind* the wells, the negatively charged DNA will simply exit the back of the well and float away into the surrounding buffer chamber.
